Female Sand grey mullet attain a maximum total length of forty centimeters [Li = forty centimeters], a size that is consistent with the moderate body proportions observed within the Mugilidae. This ultimate length is typically reached after several years of steady somatic growth in estuarine and coastal waters. Maturing individuals first exhibit gonadal development at a substantially smaller size, with puberty occurring at a total length of eighteen centimeters [Lp = eighteen centimeters]. The onset of reproductive capability at this comparatively modest length suggests an early-maturing life-history strategy, potentially an adaptation to variable recruitment conditions in temperate estuaries. Field surveys along the eastern Australian coastline have confirmed that individuals as small as eighteen centimeters can possess fully developed gonads, indicating that size at maturity is a relatively fixed trait in this species. The disparity between the length at which females first mature and their maximum recorded length implies a prolonged period of adult growth, during which individuals continue to increase in body size while simultaneously allocating resources to annual reproductive events. This pattern is common among iteroparous teleosts inhabiting seasonal environments.

The wet weight of a female at the attainment of sexual maturity has been estimated at sixty-one grams [Wwp = sixty-one grams], a body mass derived from the length-weight relationship established for this species. This estimate suggests that females have accumulated sufficient somatic reserves by the time they reach eighteen centimeters in total length to support the energetic demands of initial gametogenesis. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight for a fully grown female reaches six hundred and forty-nine grams [Wwi = six hundred and forty-nine grams], representing an approximately tenfold increase in mass from puberty to asymptotic size. This substantial post-maturation mass gain underscores the importance of continued resource acquisition during the adult stage, as females must partition energy between somatic maintenance and the production of high-fecundity clutches. The length-weight coefficient used to derive these masses follows the allometric equation typical of mugilids, and comparative data from congeners confirm that these values fall within the expected range for a medium-bodied mullet species.

Egg diameter in this species averages approximately 0.9 millimeters, and the corresponding wet weight of a single recently fertilized ovum is minuscule, calculated at 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams]. This exceedingly small egg mass is characteristic of pelagic spawning teleosts that produce large numbers of small, yolk-poor oocytes as part of a high-fecundity, low-investment-per-offspring reproductive strategy. Following fertilization, the chorionate embryo develops rapidly within the water column, and the tiny size of the egg places constraints on the initial larval energy reserves available before the onset of exogenous feeding. The yolk-sac larva that emerges at eclosion is thus highly dependent on the timely availability of suitable planktonic prey. This initial mass stands in stark contrast to the body masses of later life stages, emphasizing the dramatic scale of ontogenetic growth that must occur over the life cycle.

Reproductive output in this species has been characterized under controlled thermal conditions. At a water temperature of 21.2 °C [T = 21.2 °C], gravid females have been observed to produce a maximum of approximately 960 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 960 eggs per spawning event], with the interval between successive spawnings being roughly one day under optimal conditions, yielding a daily reproductive rate of approximately 960 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 960 eggs per day]. This high fecundity is based on data from the related congener Chelon saliens and is considered representative for Myxus elongatus under optimal thermal regimes. The temperature of 21.2 °C corresponds to late spring and summer conditions within the species' native range, when phytoplankton blooms typically sustain larval feeding success. The high reproductive output is consistent with an opportunistic life-history strategy adapted to pulsed productivity in estuarine environments. It is important to note that this maximum rate may not be sustained throughout the entire spawning season; rather, it represents the peak capacity observed under favorable conditions when metabolic demands are fully met by available prey resources.

Longevity records indicate that the maximum lifespan for Sand grey mullet is approximately twelve years [am = approximately twelve years], a duration that is relatively extended for a mugilid of this body size when maintained at a stable temperature of 21.2 °C [T = 21.2 °C]. Wild-caught individuals exhibiting advanced otolith annuli counts have confirmed that some fish exceed this age, but twelve years represents the typical maximum documented across multiple estuarine populations. This lifespan, combined with the early onset of reproduction at eighteen centimeters total length, allows for numerous reproductive seasons over the course of an individual's life. The species' iteroparous strategy, whereby females spawn repeatedly across several years, buffers against occasional recruitment failures by spreading reproductive effort over time. Long-term mark-recapture studies in southern Queensland estuaries have demonstrated that individuals aged eight to ten years still exhibit robust gonadal development, suggesting that reproductive senescence occurs very late, if at all, in this species.
